exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Marginal Distribution From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\, \sin y, & 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}2,\, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_X(x).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0\leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}2$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_0^{\pi/2} \dfrac{2}{\pi}\,\sin y \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\pi} \Big[-\cos y\Big]_{y=0}^{y=\pi/2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\left(-\cos \dfrac{\pi}2 + \cos 0\right) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{\pi}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is given by

\[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{\pi}, & 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{2}y^2, & 0 \leq x \leq 2,\, 0 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_X(x).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0\leq x \leq 2$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int^1_0 \dfrac{3}{2}y^2 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{3}{2} \left[\dfrac13 y^3\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2} \left[y^3\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}(1^3 - 0) \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is given by

\[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}, & 0 \leq x \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} e^{-(x+y)}, & x\geq 0,\, y \geq 0, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_X(x).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $x \geq 0$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_0^\infty e^{-(x+y)} \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\left[-e^{-(x+y)}\right]_{y=0}^{y=\infty} \\[5pt] &=\left(0+e^{-(x+0)}\right) \\[5pt] &=e^{-x}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is given by

\[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-x}, & x \geq 0, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

example.title: Finding a Marginal Distribution From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2-1}\sin(x+y), & 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}4,\, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}4, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_Y(y).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0\leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}4$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &=\int^{\pi/4}_0 \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2-1}\sin(x+y) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt 2-1}\big[ -\cos(x+y) \big]_{x=0}^{x=\pi/4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt 2}\big[ \cos(x+y) \big]_{x=0}^{x=\pi/4} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt 2}\left[ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}4+y\right)-\cos\left(0+y\right) \right] \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt 2}\left(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}4+y\right)-\cos y \right). \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{1-\sqrt 2}\left(\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}4+y\right)-\cos y \right), & 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}4, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

example.title: Finding a Marginal Distribution From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} e^{-\left(\frac x3+3y\right)}, & x\geq 0,\, y \geq 0, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_Y(y).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $y \geq 0$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_0^\infty e^{-\left(\frac x3+3y\right)}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\left[-3e^{-\left(\frac x3+3y\right)}\right]_{x=0}^{x=\infty} \\[5pt] &=-3\left[ e^{-\left(\frac x3+3y\right)}\right]_{x=0}^{x=\infty} \\[5pt] &=-3\left[ 0-e^{-\left(0+3y\right)}\right] \\[5pt] &=3 e^{-3y}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 3 e^{-3y}, & y \geq 0, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Finding a Marginal Probability From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{6}(x+y), & 0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 3, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find $P(Y \leq 1).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 3$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int^1_0 \dfrac{1}{6}(x+y) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6} \left[ \dfrac{x^2}{2}+xy \right]_{x=0}^{x=1}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6} \left[ \dfrac{1}{2}+y \right] - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{y}{6}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{y}{6}, & 0 \leq y \leq 3, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the required probability is

\begin{align} P(Y \leq 1) &=\int_{-\infty}^{1} f_Y(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} \left(\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{y}{6}\right) \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\left[\dfrac{y}{12}+\dfrac{y^2}{12}\right]_0^{1}\\[5pt] &=\left[\dfrac{1}{12}+\dfrac{1}{12}\right] - 0 \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{6}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Marginal Probability From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}y\sin x, & 0 \leq x \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find $P(-3 < Y < 1 ).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 2$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int^{\pi/2}_0 \dfrac{1}{2}y\sin x \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}y \big[ -\cos x \big]_{x=0}^{x=\pi/2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}y \left( -\cos \left(\dfrac{\pi}2\right)+\cos( 0) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2}y. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2}y, & 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the required probability is

\begin{align} P(-3 < Y < 1) &=\int_{-3}^{1} f_Y(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} \dfrac{1}{2}y\, \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\dfrac{y^2}{2}\right]_0^{1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}\left(1^2-0^2\right)\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Marginal Probability From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{6}\,x^3\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}, & 0 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find $P(Y \leq 1).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 2$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int^2_0\dfrac{1}{6}\,x^3\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{6}\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}\left[\dfrac14x^4\right]_{x=0}^{x=2}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{24}\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}\left[2^4-0^4\right]\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}, & 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the required probability is

\begin{align} P(Y \leq 1) &=\int_{-\infty}^{1} f_Y(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{1} \dfrac{2}{3}\sqrt[3]{\dfrac y2}\, \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{2}}\int_0^{1}\,y^{1/3} \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{2}{3\sqrt[3]{2}}\left[\dfrac34y^{4/3}\right]_0^{1}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}\left[1^{4/3}-0^{4/3}\right]\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt[3]{2}}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Marginal Probability From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{10}{3}xy^4, & 1 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find $P\left(Y < \dfrac{4}{5} \right).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int^2_1 \dfrac{10}{3}xy^4\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{10}{3}y^4\left[ \dfrac12x^2 \right]_{x=1}^{x=2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{5}{3}y^4\left( 2^2-1^2\right)\\[5pt] &= 5y^4. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 5y^4, & 0 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the required probability is

\begin{align} P\left(Y < \dfrac{4}{5} \right) &=\int_{-\infty}^{4/5} f_Y(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_0^{4/5} 5y^4\, \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\left[y^5\right]_0^{4/5}\\[5pt] &=\left( \dfrac{4}{5} \right)^{5} - 0^5 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1024}{3125}. \end{align}

example.title: Finding a Marginal Probability From a Joint Distribution

question.text: Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{16}(x^3+y^3), & 0 \leq x \leq 2, \, 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Find $P(Y \geq 1).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 2$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int^2_0 \dfrac{1}{16}(x^3+y^3)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16} \left[ \dfrac{x^4}{4}+xy^3 \right]_{x=0}^{x=2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16} \left[ \dfrac{2^4}{4}+(2)y^3 \right] - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16}\left(4+2y^3 \right)\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}y^3. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}y^3, & 0 \leq y \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

Therefore, the required probability is

\begin{align} P(Y \geq 1) &=\int^{\infty}_{1} f_Y(y) \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &=\int_1^{2} \left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\dfrac{1}{8}y^3\right) \textrm{d}y\\[5pt] &=\left[\dfrac{1}{4}y+\dfrac{1}{32}y^4\right]_1^{2}\\[5pt] &=\left[\dfrac{1}{4}(2)+\dfrac{1}{32}2^4\right]-\left[\dfrac{1}{4}(1)+\dfrac{1}{32}1^4\right]\\[5pt] &=1-\dfrac9{32}\\[5pt] &=\dfrac{23}{32}. \end{align}

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with a joint probability density function

\[ f(x,y) = \dfrac{3x}{2(y^2+1)}, \quad y^2 \leq x \leq 1. \]

Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_Y(y).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

First, let's sketch the region $D = \{(x,y) \::\: y^2 \leq x \leq1\}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $-1 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{y^2}^{1} \dfrac{3x}{2(y^2+1)}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2(y^2+1)} \int_{y^2}^{1} x \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2(y^2+1)} \left[ \dfrac12x^2\right]_{x=y^2}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4(y^2+1)} \left[1-\left(y^2\right)^2 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{4(y^2+1)} \left[1-y^4 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3(1-y^2)(1+y^2)}{4(y^2+1)} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3(1-y^2)}{4} \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{3(1-y^2)}{4}, & -1 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with a joint probability density function

$$ f(x,y)=\dfrac12xy,\quad 0 \leq x\leq y \leq 2. $$ Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_X(x).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

First, let's sketch the region $D = \{(x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x\leq y \leq 2 \}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0 \leq x \leq 2$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_x^2 \dfrac{1}{2} xy \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \int_x^2 xy \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left[\dfrac12xy^2\right]_{y=x}^{y=2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \left[xy^2\right]_{y=x}^{y=2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \left[x\cdot 2^2 - x\cdot x^2\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{4} \left[4x - x^3\right] \\[5pt] &= x - \dfrac14x^3. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is given by

\[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} x - \dfrac14x^3, & 0 \leq x \leq 2, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with a joint probability density function

\[ f(x,y) = 3 \left( x^2 + y^2 \right), \quad 0 \leq y \leq x \leq 1. \]

Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_Y(y).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

First, let's sketch the region $D = \{(x,y) \::\: 0 \leq y \leq x \leq 1 \}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{y}^{1}3 \left( x^2 + y^2 \right)\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3 \int_{y}^{1} \left( x^2 + y^2 \right) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 3 \left[ \dfrac13x^3+xy^2\right]_{x=y}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= \left[x^3 + 3xy^2\right]_{x=y}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= \left[(1^3+3\cdot 1 \cdot y^2) - (y^3+3\cdot y \cdot y^2) \right] \\[5pt] &= 1+3y^2-4y^3. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} 1+3y^2-4y^3, & 0 \leq y \leq 1, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with a joint probability density function

\[ f(x,y) = \dfrac{1}{16}xy^3 , \quad 0 \leq x \leq 4,\quad 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt{x}. \]

Find the expression for the marginal PDF $f_X(x).$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

First, let's sketch the region $D = \{(x,y) \::\: 0 \leq x \leq 4, 0 \leq y \leq \sqrt{x} \}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $0 \leq x \leq 4$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_{0}^{\sqrt{x}} \dfrac{1}{16} xy^3 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16} \int_{0}^{\sqrt{x}} x y^3 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{16} \left[ \dfrac14xy^4\right]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{64} \left[xy^4\right]_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{64} \left[x\cdot (\sqrt{x})^4 - x\cdot (\sqrt{0})^4\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{64} \left[x\cdot x^2 - 0\right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3}{64}. \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_X(x)$ is given by

\[ f_X(x) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{x^3}{64}, & 0 \leq x \leq 4, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

First, let's sketch the region $D = \{(x,y) \::\: x \geq 0,\, y \leq -x^2 \}.$

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $y \leq 0$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{0}^{\sqrt{-y}} 2xe^y \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2 \int_{0}^{\sqrt{-y}} xe^y \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2 \left[ \dfrac12 x^2e^y\right]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{-y}} \\[5pt] &= \big[x^2e^y\big]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{-y}} \\[5pt] &= \left[\left(\sqrt{-y}\right)^2\cdot e^y - 0^2\cdot e^y\right] \\[5pt] &= -ye^y . \end{align}

Therefore, the full expression for $f_Y(y)$ is given by

\[ f_Y(y) = \begin{cases} -ye^y , & y \leq 0, \\[5pt] 0, & \textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{3}{2}(x^2+y^2), & {0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1}, \\[5pt] 0,&\textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The marginal CDF $F_Y(y)$ of $Y$ is given by

\[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] g(y), &0\leq y \leq 1\\[5pt] 1 &y\gt 1. \end{cases} \]

What is the function $g(y)?$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{0}^1 \dfrac{3}{2}(x^2+y^2) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \int_{0}^{1} (x^2+y^2) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left[ \dfrac13 x^3 + xy^2 \right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left[ \dfrac13 \cdot1^3 + 1 \cdot y^2 - 0 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{2} \left( \dfrac13 + y^2 \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12+\dfrac{3y^2}{2}. \end{align}

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} F_Y(y) &= \int_{-\infty}^{y} f_Y(u) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{y}\left( \dfrac12+\dfrac{3u^2}{2}\right) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{u}{2}+\dfrac{u^3}{2} \right]_0^y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ y+y^3 - 0 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y+y^3}{2}. \end{align}

So, the full expression for $F_Y(y)$ is

\[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y+y^3}{2}, &0\leq y \leq 1\\[5pt] 1 & y\gt 1. \end{cases} \]

Finally, $g(y) = \dfrac{y+y^3}{2}.$

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} e^{-(x+y)}, & { x \geq 0, \, y \geq 0}, \\[5pt] 0,&\textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The marginal CDF $F_X(x)$ of $X$ is given by

\[ F_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x\lt 0 \\[5pt] g(x), & x \geq 0. \end{cases} \]

What is the function $g(x)?$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $ x \geq 0$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-(x+y)}\, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= e^{-x} \lim_{b\to\infty}\int_{0}^{b} e^{-y}\, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= e^{-x} \lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-e^{-y}\right]_{y=0}^{y=b} \\[5pt] &= e^{-x} \lim_{b\to\infty}\left(1-e^{-b}\right) \\[5pt] &= e^{-x} . \end{align}

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $X$ for $ x \geq 0$ is

\begin{align} F_X(x) &= \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(u) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{x} e^{-u} \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \left[ - e^{-u} \right]_0^x \\[5pt] &= 1 -e^{-x}. \end{align}

So, the full expression for $F_X(x)$ is

\[ F_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x\lt 0 \\[5pt] 1-e^{-x}, & x \geq 0. \end{cases} \]

Finally, $g(x) = 1-e^{-x}.$

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{3y^2}{x^2}, & { x \geq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1}, \\[5pt] 0,&\textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The marginal CDF $F_X(x)$ of $X$ is given by

\[ F_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x\lt 1 \\[5pt] g(x), & x \geq 1. \end{cases} \]

What is the function $g(x)?$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $X$ for $ x \geq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_X(x) &= \int_{0}^1 \dfrac{3y^2}{x^2} \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{x^2}\int_{0}^1y^2 \, \textrm{d}y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{3}{x^2} \left[\dfrac{y^3}{3}\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{x^2} \left[y^3\right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{x^2} (1^3 - 0) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{x^2} . \end{align}

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $X$ for $x \geq 1$ is

\begin{align} F_X(x) &= \int_{-\infty}^{x} f_X(u) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{1}^{x} \dfrac{1}{u^2} \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{u} \right]_1^x \\[5pt] &= 1-\dfrac{1}{x}. \end{align}

So, the full expression for $F_X(x)$ is

\[ F_X(x)= \begin{cases} 0, & x\lt 1 \\[5pt] 1-\dfrac{1}{x}, & x \geq 1. \end{cases} \]

Finally, $g(x) = 1-\dfrac{1}{x}.$

question.text:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} \dfrac{2y}{(x+1)^2}, & { x \geq 0, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1}, \\[5pt] 0,&\textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The marginal CDF $F_Y(y)$ of $Y$ is given by

\[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] g(y), & 0 \leq y \leq 1 \\[5pt] 1, & y \gt 1. \end{cases} \]

What is the function $g(y)?$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

\begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{0}^{\infty} \dfrac{2y}{(x+1)^2} \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2y \lim_{b\to\infty}\int_{0}^{b} \dfrac{1}{(x+1)^2}\, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= 2y \lim_{b\to\infty}\left[-\dfrac{1}{(x+1)} \right]_{0}^{b} \\[5pt] &= 2y \lim_{b\to\infty}\left(1-\dfrac{1}{b+1} \right) \\[5pt] &= 2y . \end{align}

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is

\begin{align} F_Y(y) &= \int_{-\infty}^{y} f_X(u) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{y} 2u \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \left[u^2\right]_0^y\\[5pt] &= y^2 - 0\\[5pt] &= y^2. \end{align}

So, the full expression for $F_Y(y)$ is

\[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] y^2 & 0 \leq y \leq 1 \\[5pt] 1, & y \gt 1. \end{cases} \]

Finally, $g(y) = y^2.$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function \[ f(x,y)= \begin{cases} x+y, & {0 \leq x \leq 1, \, 0 \leq y \leq 1}, \\[5pt] 0,&\textrm{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The marginal CDF $F_Y(y)$ of $Y$ is given by \[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] g(y), &0\leq y \leq 1\\[5pt] 1 &y\gt 1. \end{cases} \]

What is the function $g(y)?$
question.explanation:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x, y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are \begin{align*} f_X(x) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}y, \qquad f_Y(y) = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f (x, y) \, \textrm{d}x. \end{align*}

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is \begin{align} f_Y(y) &= \int_{0}^1 (x+y ) \, \textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac12 x^2 + xy \right]_{x=0}^{x=1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12 \cdot 1^2 + 1\cdot y - 0 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac12+y. \end{align}

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $Y$ for $0 \leq y \leq 1$ is \begin{align} F_Y(y) &= \int_{-\infty}^{y} f_Y(u) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{y}\left( \dfrac12+u\right) \, \textrm{d}u \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{u}{2}+\dfrac{u^2}{2} \right]_0^y \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} \left[ y+y^2 - 0 \right] \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{y+y^2}{2}. \end{align}

So, the full expression for $F_Y(y)$ is \[ F_Y(y)= \begin{cases} 0, & y\lt 0 \\[5pt] \dfrac{y+y^2}{2}, &0\leq y \leq 1\\[5pt] 1 & y\gt 1. \end{cases} \]

Finally, $g(y) = \dfrac{y+y^2}{2}.$
